### page_1
Geophys. J. R. asb. SOC.( 1979) 59,101-122
The palaeomagnetism of the central zone of the
Lewisian foreland, north-west Scotland
J. D. A. Piper Sub-department of Geophysics, University of Liverpool,
Liverpool L69 3BX
Received 1979 March 3; in original form 1978 November 1
Summary. Three principal directions of magnetization are recognized in
the central part of the Lewisian metamorphic terrain of north-west Scotland.
The first ('A') magnetization is a high blocking temperature component
residing in magnetite and imposed during post-Laxfordian uplift and
cooling. Fifty sites yield an overall mean D = 285.9", I = 54.9" and palaeo-
magnetic pole at 273.2' E, 37.6" N (dp = 3.7", dm = 5.2"); this magnetization
was probably acquired at crustal depths of 6-10 km and is linked to K--Ar
uplift ages averaging 1650-1 625 Ma. The second ('B') magnetizations are
defined by E-W directions and also reside in high blocking temperature
components; they are, however, dipolar, have some properties distinct from
the 'A' magnetizations, and are correlated with late stages in the history of
the complex at 1400-1200 Ma. The third ('C') NE directed magnetizations
reside predominantly in low blocking temperature components in pyrrhotite
and possibly maghemite, and were probably acquired at a late stage of the
regional uplift; they do not correlate with post-1450 Ma magnetizations from
the Laurentian Shield and probably relate to the as yet undefined interval
1600-1450 Ma. The collective palaeomagnetic data and certain geologic
data suggest that the Lewisian foreland should be rotated by 30" clockwise
about a local axis of rotation on the conventional reconstructicn of the North
Atlantic continents; this rotation is associated with Lower Palaeozoic trans-
current movements and may be related to a fourth ('D') magnetization of
viscous origin.
A collective assessment of 1850-1 600 Ma palaeomagnetic data for the
Laurentian Shield defines a large apw loop; there is widespread agreement
between data from the constituent structural provinces of the Shield although
different metamorphic regions define complementary segments of the loop
related to uplift over different intervals of time.
1 Introduction
The present decade has seen an extension of the general field of Precambrian palaeo-
magnetism into the study of metamorphic basement regions. It is recognized that these

terrains retain a complex record of magnetizations acquired at different times. The cooling
of these rocks has generally taken place so slowly that components of secular variation will
be averaged and under favourable circumstances apparent polar wander (apw) movement
may be recorded within individual samples (Morgan 1976a). While these terrains can,
therefore, yield a very valuable record of apw movements, they present at first a major
practical problem of evaluating techniques to recover the complete record of magnetizations
present and, secondly, an interpretational problem in relating these magnetizations to the
complex geochronological record of Precambrian metamorphism, uplift and cooling.
This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of such a terrain comprising the central part of
the Lewisian foreland of NW Scotland. In Proterozoic times this formed a peripheral part of
the much larger Laurentian Shield, a cratonic region comprising the Precambrian basement
of North America and Greenland (Bridgwater, Watson & Windley 1973).
2 Geology
2.1 REGIONAL SETTING
The Precambrian Lewisian basement of NW Scotland, which includes the mainland north of
Skye and the Outer Hebrides, forms a foreland zone to the Caledonian orogenic belt
(c. 550-380 Ma). It comprises quartzo-feldspathic gneisses affected by amphibolite/
granulite metamorphism during an early Scourian episode of crustal incrementation and
metamorphism, known as the Badcallian, at approximately 2900--2700 Ma (Moorbath,
Welke & Gale 1969); little new material has been added to the complex since this episode
(Watson 1975). More restricted reactivation of the Lewisian took place during a late
Scourian (Inverian) episode at c. 2300-2200 Ma, and widespread intrusion of NW-SE dykes
took place in late- and post-Inverian times; these are predominantly tholeiitic in
composition but include a later suite of picrite dykes in addition to a number of other
compositions. The dykes were first used by Sutton &Watson (1951) to separate a pre-dyke
(Scourian) mobile episode from a post-dyke (Laxfordian) mobile episode. They are now
wholly or partly amphibolitized, and are foliated to variable degrees in those parts of the
Lewisian affected by the Laxfordian episode, although some relict igneous textures are
usually present.
The Laxfordian episode included widespread metamorphism predominantly to an
amphibolite facies and associated with migmatization and intrusion of granites and
pegmatites; it probably reached a climax at about 1850 Ma but a protracted history of uplift
and cooling followed the event. In the type area of Loch Laxford the Laxfordian comprises
Lewisian rocks affected by episodic thermal/tectonic activity between c. 2800 and 1700 Ma
and contrasts with the adjacent Scourian terrain where regional thermal/tectonic activity
ceased at about 2700 Ma (Watson 1975).
2.2 SCOURIAN-LAXFORDIAN RELATIONSHIPS AND HISTORY OF UPLIFT
The relationship between these two contrasting zones is critical to the interpretation of
palaeomagnetic data from the two regions and to linking these data with the history of
uplift. The early work of Peach et al. (1907) suggested that the parent rocks of the
Laxfordian complex were similar to the Scourian complex, a view supported by Sutton &
Watson (1 95 1); these workers attributed the distinctive characteristics of the Laxfordian
zones to deep seated reworking in postBadcallian times. Davies & Watson (1977) drew
comparisons between a wide range of features in the Scourian complexes and their reworked
equivalents in the Laxfordian, but there is no conclusive evidence bearing on the nature of

Palaeomagnetism of the Lewisian foreland 103
vertical movements between the Scourian and Laxfordian, and the geochemical differences
between the two areas might result either from a difference in crustal level (Tarney, Skinner
& Sheraton 1972; Sheraton, Skinner & Tarney 1973) or to migmatization (Sutton &Watson
195 1) associated with granite and pegmatite injection near the climax of the Laxfordian
episode.
The metamorphic assemblages within the dyke suite show that they were intruded into a
hot crust, probably at very great depths (O’Hara 1961 ;T arney 1968; Dearnley 1973). Davies
& Watson (1 977) quote a minimum depth of 20 km in late Scourian/early Laxfordian times
and O’Hara (1 975) suggests formation pressures of 13 kbar for Scourian granulites; if this
pressure is lithostatic it would be equivalent to crustal depths of 30-40 km (Watson 1977).
Tarney (1968) suggests that the dyke emplacement took place at depths of 15-20 km and
temperatures of c. 500°C. Dickinson & Watson (1976) have also examined disequilibrium
metamorphic reactions as an indicator of crustal depth, and identified a trend (which
includes the episodes of dyke intrusion) of progressively declining pressures during
successively later metamorphic events, with temperatures declining significantly only
towards the close of the Laxfordian event; a tentative vertical displacement of 15-20 km
is indicated with a cover of thickness of 10-15 km by late Laxfordian times. This latter
thickness had clearly been completely eroded by the time of deposition of the Stoer Group
(Torridonian) sediments at c. 1000 Ma.
2.3 GEOCHRONOLOGY*
The difference in age between the Scourian and Laxfordian episodes was first defined by
Giletti, Moorbath & Lambert (1961); these workers dated Scourian and Laxfordian
pegmatites at 2490 and 1660Ma and defined the broad interval during which the dyke
intrusion took place. Evans (1964) subsequently dated pegmatites of the Lochinver area at
2335 Ma (U-Pb) thus narrowing these limits, and in a further study dealing specifically with
the dykes of the Assynt area (covered by this study) Evans & Tarney (1964) dated a picrite
dyke near Lochinver at 2273; K-Ar ages for dolerite dykes predating the picrites ranged
from 3860-1550 Ma but the age of intrusion is restricted by the other data to the approxi-
mate interval 2335-2273 Ma. Of particular relevance to the palaeomagnetic study are the
K-Ar ages of 1630-1390 Ma from completely amphibolitized rocks in areas affected by
Laxfordian events. The thermal history of late- and post-Laxfordian times may well have
been a complex one; in the Outer Hebrides for example this interval is recorded by Rb-Sr
mineral ages of 1654-1483 Ma (Lambert, Myers & Watson 1970) and by K-Ar whole rock
ages of 1729-1510Ma (Lambert, Evans & Dearnley 1970). In the southern part of the
Lewisian mainland, Moorbath & Park (1972) date three events following dyke intrusion, the
last of these being a pegmatite emplacement at 1420 Ma; indeed mineral age determinations
from the Laxfordian show a scatter of dates down to 1400 Ma and locally to 1100 Ma
suggesting a complex, and possibly diachronous, history of uplift (Watson 1975).
2.4 SCOPE OF THE PRESENT SURVEY
The present study covers that part of the Lewisian foreland distinguished as the Central
Zone (Peach et al. 1907; Sutton & Watson 1951) where Scourian structures are extensively
preserved; the effects of the Laxfordian episode are largely restricted to narrow shear belts
and the dykes are normally discordant with the pre-dyke foliation. The sampling was

concentrated on the mafic units, mainly dykes, both because these are likely to have the
highest ferrimagnetic content and because they possess the least tectonic fabric; since
corrections to the magnetic vector become very considerable for large anisotropy of
susceptibility (Beckmann, Olsen & Sorensen 1977) and since the contribution to the
resultant susceptibility of the constituents carrying the stable remanence is uncertain (Irving
& Park 1972a), it appears advisable to avoid highly anisotropic rocks in magnetic directional
studies of metamorphic complexes.
Because the regional temperatures remained high until the close of the Laxfordian
thermal/tectonic episodes, there are no grounds for regarding any magnetizations recovered
from the Lewisian rocks as relating to the time of intrusion, indeed it is unlikely that any
such magnetizations were ever imposed because, under conditions of elevated temperature
followed by protracted cooling, the critical range of blocking temperatures is greatly lowered
(hllaiah et al. 1975) and will be much lower than the blocking temperature range defined
by short-term laboratory experiments. It is probable that regional uplift following the
Laxfordian tectonism was so slow that blocking temperature ranges were comparable to the
temperatures at which common metamorphic minerals become closed isotopic systems.
K-Ar ages for hornblende and biotite in areas of Laxfordian metamorphism average 1650-
1625 Ma (Dickinson & Watson 1976); a temperature of 250°C might be assumed for this
time but it would be unwise to correlate magnetizations and K-Ar ages precisely both
because the actual blocking temperatures are unknown and because the effects of slow
cooling on the closure of isotopic systems are only partly understood.
3 Palaeomagnetic results
3.1 THE PALAEOMAGNETIC COLLECTION
The location of the palaeomagnetic sites is given in Fig. 1 and the National Grid references
are listed in Table 1. One site typically comprises five to seven samples distributed over
several metres of outcrop and drilled in the field; most orientations were made by taking
sights on the Sun and the remainder were made using magnetic compass in conjunction with
topographic sights.
It is necessary to evaluate the most appropriate practical cleaning techniques for treating
slowly cooled rocks for each individual collection. Although these rocks have acquired their
magnetic movements during a prolonged thermal process, alternating field (af) cleaning may
be equally or more effective than thermal cleaning because the coercivity of magnetic grains
is related to their blocking temperatures by the formulae for the relaxation time of a single
domain grain (McElhinny 1973). Thermal demagnetization is, however, the only technique
which can yield information on the spectrum of blocking temperatures present and is also
the only effective method for recovering magnetic components residing in hematite.
The thermomagnetic studies (data summarized in Tables 1 and 2) show that the
magnetizations of the Lewisian complex reside predominantly in magnetite or minerals with
lower blocking temperatures, although hematite has been identified at a few sites. The af
procedure has accordingly been employed here as the principal method for treating this
collection although thermal demagnetization of one or more samples from each site has been
undertaken to define blocking temperature ranges and to ascertain whether components
had been missed by the af method. The af demagnetization was undertaken with a 500c/s
system through which the ambient magnetic field was regularly and carefully annulled, and
it utilized steps of 5 to 10 milli-Tesla (mT) up to peak field of 150 mT or to fields at which
the magnetizations could no longer be accurately measured; thermal demagnetization was
undertaken in steps of 100°C reduced to 30°C near the Curie points using a commercial

Schonstedt demagnetizer. In addition a number of samples were subjected to a two-stage
treatment (Park 1975) of af followed by thermal treatment. Thermomagnetic de-
terminations (saturation magnetization, J,, versus temperature) were found to be particularly
useful in identifying separate components of magnetization; one determination was made
from each site and additional determinations were made where more than one component
of magnetization was identified.
3.2 Y AL AEO M A G N ET IC R E su LTS
The majority of the sites from this collection (40 out of 62) yield either one single direction
of magnetization with a moderate positive inclination and westerly declination, or have this
direction as one component. The sites in which this is the only component are typically
highly stable to af demagnetization and exhibit slight and systematic movement over the
range of treatment (0-150 mT); at low fields of 5-25 mT samples cease to move along a
great circle path through the present Earth’s field direction (Fig. 2) and sample directions
have been compounded at this stage to calculate site means (Table 1). These magnetizations
isolated by af treatment are stable to subsequent thermal demagnetization (Fig. 2): the
directions do not change and residual moments do not fall appreciably until the Curie
points are approached at 530-560°C. A number of paired cylinders from the same field
core have been thermally and af cleaned to compare the efficiency of the two techniques in
isolating this remanence. Typical examples are illustrated in Fig. 2 (sites 39 and 53): stable
end points reached by af demagnetization at 10mT are not achieved by thermal
demagnetization until temperatures of 400-500°C. Morgan (1 976b) observed this behaviour
in the demagnetization of magnetite-bearing basement rocks, and has utilized the two sets
of curves of Evans & McElhinny (1 969) relating blocking temperatures and unblocking fields
to magnetite grain dimensions to provide a physical explanation: the unblocking field curves

cut across the unblocking temperature curves so that a given af demagnetization field can
demagnetize grains with a very wide spectrum of blocking temperatures; in addition,
depending on the distribution of grain sizes present, a given af field will selectively de-
magnetize more grains with lower blocking temperatures than with higher blocking
temperatures.
The stable samples with single component magnetizations all give simple thermomagnetic
spectra of the type shown in Fig. 4 (sites 24, 62) with single Curie points with the range
5 15-550'C attributable to titanomagnetite; in most cases, as in the examples illustrated in
Fig. 4, the curves are completely reversible (Table 1).
The sites falling in this group with single, high coercivity, hgh blocking temperature
remanence are listed in Table 1 and are given the collective designation of 'A' magnetiza-
tions to distinguish them from other less well-defined, and probably younger,
magnetizations described below. Twenty-four sites falling in this group (2, 3, 9, 12, 14,
24-26, 28, 30, 34, 38, 40, 45, 49, 50, 52-55, 57, 60-62) yield simple reversible thermo-
magnetic spectra with a single high Curie point attributable to titanomagnetites. Six further
sites in this group (10, 11, 16, 29, 41 and 42) show a significant drop in saturation
magnetization below about 300'C (as illustrated by sites 29 and 42, Fig. 4) followed by a
single high Curie point curve typical of the other sites; this component must undergo
alteration on heating because saturation remanence increases to variable degrees on cooling
and the curves are not reversible; no low blocking temperature component has, however,
been identified at these sites. By contrast a further 10 sites (5,8,13,19,20,22,37,39,44
and 47), all of which have these more complex thermomagnetic spectra, do show a low
blocking temperature component in some or all samples from the same site; in most cases
this can be removed by progressive af and/or thermal cleaning to recover a group 'A'
direction. The significance of these components is considered below but since the 'A'
direction is recovered in all cases at the higher field or temperature, it is regarded as
representing the primary component and these sites are therefore combined with the re-
maining 3 1 sites in Table 1.
The overall mean is D = 286.0', Z = 54.7' yielding a palaeomagnetic pole at 272.9" E,
37.5' N (dp = 4.4', dm = 6.2'). In an earlier study of the Lewisian dykes, Beckmann (1976)
found 10 sites in this area yielding group 'A' magnetizations including all the sites with
highest coercivities of magnetization; it is possible that this magnetization was also present
in some of his 28 remaining sites, but the demagnetizing apparatus used was inadequate to
resolve this in samples with low magnetic coercivities. Although some of the rock units
sampled in this study are the same as those sampled by Beckmann it is legitimate to
combine them by giving unit weight to each site because the magnetizations derive from
metamorphic rocks cooled over long periods of time. The mean (Table 1) of all 50 sites is
then D = 285.9', I=5 4.9', yielding a palaeomagnetic pole for the central part of the
Lewisian foreland of 273.2" E, 37.6" N (dp = 3.7', dm = 5.2').
A second series of sites listed in Table 2 is defined as group 'B', although since the sites
belonging to this group are not collectively well grouped their nature is much more difficult
to decipher. They are regarded as a high blocking temperature group because they yield
directions stable to thermal treatment and high Curie points attributable to titanomagnetite
and hematite (sites 17 and 31) but their behaviour to af demagnetization is in general quite
different from the group 'A' demagnetization. Instead of moving to a single stable end point
sample directions migrate progressively along irregular paths over the whole range of af
treatment (Fig. 5). Also two polarities appear to be present: sites 27, 47 and 48 are anti-
parallel to sites 17, 18 and 19 and sites 4 and 58 are approximately antiparallel to site 17.
At sites 19 and 47 group 'A' magnetizations (site 17) are present in separate samples from

the same site and both have comparable properties. There is also some suggestion of an
overlap between the two groups because a few sites included in group 'A' have a wide range of
magnetic inclinations present at one site; this applies notably at site 24 (Table 1) where a
narrow range of declinations but a wide range of inclinations result in a low overall value
of the precision parameter k. Site 48 (Table 2) has shallow negative inclinations and with
progressive demagnetization some samples move to steeper negative inclinations; this site
also exhibits two distinct Curie points attributable to titanomagnetite (500 and 530°C).
The presence of antiparallel directions is noteworthy: Beckmann (1976) considered that the
Lewisian rocks were unlikely to have been magnetized during slow cooling because, in a
reversing field, they would successively acquire a sequence of antiparallel components as
they cooled through their blocking temperature ranges. It is necessary to postulate either an
alternative mechanism (Beckmann considered a shock induced remanence related to seismic
events) or that the prevailing magnetic field was predominantly of one polarity. Morgan
(1 976c) considered that a protracted magnetization during slow uplift and cooling is the
only tenable mechanism applicable to the Lewisian terrain, and it is the only one which can
clearly be related to the geological history outlined in Section 2.
In Table 2 the 'B' magnetizations are combined together into two groups as antiparallel
sites 4, 17 and 58 (Bl) and antiparallel sites 18, 19, 27, 31, 47 and 48 (B2); it is not
suggested that this is the only way of treating the data because they do not form a compact
group (Fig. 7) and they may not represent a coherent geological event; to define their real

significance would require a more detailed sample even than that achieved in the present
study. Beckmann (1976) identified a single dyke at Badcall near Scourie with a stable
magnetization removed from the group ‘A’ directions of D = 106.1”, Z = 1. O” (k = 35) and
similar to the group ‘B’ directions of this study; this dyke was dated by Evans & Tarney
(1964) at 1873 Ma in its least altered part and 1450 Mainanamphibolitized region defining
probable limits to the age of magnetization.
We may observe in passing the identification of similar ‘B’ magnetizations at adjacent
basic bodies (18, 19, 47, 48 A) and the location of ‘B’ magnetizations of dyke site 58
between four dykes showing group ‘A’ magnetizations; this suggests that tracts of country
including more than one dyke may record magnetizations of different age from the
surrounding terrain, and presumably the temperature at which a magnetization was acquired
will depend both on compositional variations and on cooling conditions, in particular the
presence of fluids and the proximity to shear zones. However, one further possibility is that
a much later phase of dyke intrusion is present within the foreland to account for the
‘B’ magnetizations; to date no clear petrologic or radiometric evidence for a younger dyke
swarm is available.
One further group of directions defined by this study has NE declinations and positive
inclinations (Fig. 7) and is classed here as group ‘C’ with properties summarized in Table 2.
Two of the sites falling in this grouping (6 and 59, Fig. 2) have single high blocking tempera-
ture components, while at sites 7, 15, 21, 23, 32, 35, 36,43 and 51 a similar direction is
present as the only magnetization present at these weakly magnetized sites (Fig. 3, Table 2).
At five sites (8, 20, 22, 39,44) this component is identified in some samples although ‘A’
magnetizations are also present at these sites; in general these magnetizations are not
identified in the same specimen although a few samples (e.g. site 44, Fig. 2) show a move-
ment to group ‘A’ directions with progressive demagnetization. Thermal demagnetization
and thermomagnetic results show that sites 6 and 59 and probably 20 and 32 have this
component residing in titanomagnetite, but this does not appear to be the case at most of
the remaining sites which show a rapid and exponential loss of J, and magnetic moments
which become too weak to measure after thermal treatment at 300-400°C (32, Fig. 2).
The low blocking temperature ‘C’ components might reside in either pyrrhotite
(Fe ,S) of maghemite (yFe203). Since the latter mineral converts continuously to
-
crFe20, on heating over the range 300-700°C it is a possible contender at least at site 39

### page_11
Palaeomagnetism of the Lewisian foreland 111
blocking temperature components have also been identified from other Precambrian terrains
(e.g. McGlynn & Irving 1978) but they present a particular physical problem because they
lie at the lower end of the range of magnetizations which could possibly survive from Lower
Proterozoic times. Studies of the variation in relaxation time with temperature (Chamalaun
1964; McElhinny 1973) show that magnetic grains with blocking temperatures of 280°C
would, at surface temperatures, have a relaxation time of only 100 Ma while grains with
slightly higher blocking temperature of 310'C would have a relaxation time of over
l000Ma. Although pyrrhotite loses the bulk of its remanence by 300°C (Nagata 1961)
it undergoes a NBel-type transition at approximately 3 10°C (Bhimasankaram 1964) and
retains weak ferrimagnetic properties to 560°C. It may thus be considered in the context
of Precambrian magnetizations and is a prominent constituent of some of the Lewisian
rocks (next section).
In view of the differing origin of the magnetizations falling in the 'C' group, they may be
of different ages and it is not strictly correct to combine them into a single mean; also they
show a non-Fisherian distribution which is smeared towards the primitive (Fig. 7). However,
for the purposes of discussion the 14 better grouped directions with moderate positive
inclinations have been combined in Table 2 to yield a mean D = 42", I = 40' representative
of this direction of magnetization.
Four sites (13, 16, 23 and 37) and a few individual specimens'from several other sites
show a SE positive component of viscous remanent magnetization which is always removed
by af demagnetization in low fields (Fig. 5). This direction (mean D = 161", I= 48' (four
sites, k = 115) palaeomagnetic pole at 11' E, 1' S) is worthy of note because it is the only
one from this study which closely correlates with (post-Cambrian) Lower Palaeozoic palaeo-
field directions for Britain. It is similar to Ordovician palaeofield directions for Britain south
of Aberdeenshire and (with the possible exception of sites 46 and 56, Table 2) the only
evidence for remagnetization during Palaeozoic orogenic activity within the adjacent
Caledonian belt.

The present study was oriented towards possible petrologic differences between the
specimens carrying 'A', 'B' and 'C' magnetizations. The 'A' group sites which are both
strongly magnetized and highly stable (e.g. 19, 20, 59-62) contain variable amounts of
pyrite and two phases of titanomagnetite as large homogeneous grains with little or no
marginal alteration and numerous fine rods (c. 1 x 2 0 p )o riented along cleavage planes in
silicate phases; this latter phase is widely reported as a carrier of stable high coercivity NRM
(e.g. Evans, McElhinny & Gifford 1968). Other samples exhibit more complex phases with
patchy alteration of titanomagnetite to hematite/rutile aggregates (sites 38 and 57) or a
clothwork texture with development of spinel rods (1 1). The weakly magnetized sites in
general exhibit a very sparse opaque content while all samples yielding type D thermo-
magnetic curves exhibit magnetite associated with thick rims of maghemite. In general the

4.1 AGE OF THE MAGNETIZATIONS
The magnetizations recognized in these Lewisian rocks yield the estimates of palaeomagnetic
poles listed in Tables 1 and 2; the pole derived from the ‘A’ magnetization is regarded as the
oldest because this magnetization resides in primary titanomagnetite associated with silicate
phases. It is not possible to identify with certainty the age relationships of the ‘B’ and ‘C’
magnetizations; however, the ‘C’ magnetizations are of one polarity only and, since they
are carried by pyrrhotite at some sites and probably by maghemite at others, they could
have been acquired at a late stage in the uplift and cooling of the metamorphic complex
or possibly during later reheating.
In the absence of a knowledge of the rate of cooling, it is also not possible to calculate
precisely the reduction of the blocking temperature range with slow cooling, but the calcula-
tions of Pullaiah et al. (1975) show that it is reasonable to assume that the blocking tempera-
ture ranges averaging 570-470°C were depressed to c. 250-150°C for those rocks cooled
during uplift over periods in excess of lO’yr (Dickinson & Watson 1976). These tempera-
tures would only have been achieved at late stages in the post-Laxfordian uplift and cooling
by which time-temperature gradients of 45”C/km achieved at the climax of the Laxfordian
episode (Dickinson & Watson 1976) would have been reduced to perhaps 25”Clkm. This
implies that the magnetizations were imposed at crustal depths of 6-10 km and the higher
end of this temperature range (relevant to the ‘A’ magnetizations) is defined by K-Ar
mineral dates averaging 1650-1625 Ma (Dickinson & Watson 1976). The lower end of this
Downloaded

4.2 RELATIONSHIPO F LEWISIAN DATA TO PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS FROM
THE LAURENTIAN SHIELD
To compare the Lewisian magnetizations with contemporaneous results from elsewhere in
the Laurentian Craton, the palaeomagnetic poles are listed in Table 3 after rotation
according to the continental reconstruction of Bullard, Everett & Smith (1 965); this corrects
for Phanerozoic drift. Although this reconstruction has been widely used to interpret palaeo-
magnetic data from NW Scotland, it should not be accepted unequivocally for two reasons:
first, although the Ketilidian belt of south Greenland has some analogies with the
Laxfordian, no continuation of the Archaean nucleus of central-southern Greenland is
identified in the Lewisian foreland; secondly, prior to 390 Ma there is a major discrepancy
between the palaeomagnetic results from Britain and from North Arnerica/Continental
Europe on the Pangaean reconstruction (Morris 1976; Piper, in preparation). Tlus anomaly
is only known to apply to Britain south of the Great Glen Fault but it is possible that the
hypothesized zones of sinistral strike-slip motion necessary to account for this discrepancy
using tectonic models lie outside of the Caledonian belt and within the Precambrian fore-
land. Indeed, in a major reassessment of Upper Proterozoic palaeomagnetic data Stearn
(1978) finds that these Upper Proterozoic palaeomagnetic data only agree precisely with
contemporaneous Laurentian and Baltic Shield data if the Lewisian foreland is rotated by
30" clockwise about a local axis of rotation. Such a motion is consistent with the large-scale
strike-slip motions along the orthotectonic Caledonides inferred from Palaeozoic data and
should be identifiable from the alignment of major Precambrian features within the foreland.
The Scourie dykes (average trend 120-125" E) are part of a larger conjugate swarm found in
Greenland and Labrador (Escher, Jack & Watterson 1976). In west Greenland these dykes
have a trend averaging 100" E while in the same (Nagssugtuqidian) belt in east Greenland the
trend is 120--125" E. On the Bullard et al. (1965) reconstruction the Scourie dykes strike
approximately 20" further to the east of the east Greenland dykes, but if the foreland is
rotated by 30" clockwise this is reduced to 10" to the west. There is thus some geological
evidence for Stearn's (1978) conclusions from the palaeomagnetic data, and the Lewisian
palaeomagnetic pole is plotted in Fig. 8 both before and after a local rotation of 30". It will
be noted that the Lewisian 'A' magnetizations then agree more closely with the con-
temporaneous Ketilidian poles from south Greenland.
4.3 MIDDLE-LOWER PROTEROZOIC APW RELATIVE TO THE LAURENTIAN SHIELD
To evaluate the significance of the Lewisian results in the context of Laurentian palaeo-
magnetic poles, the collective data for the interval 1850-1400 Ma are tabulated in Table 3
and plotted in Fig. 8. Since no magnetization from the Lewisian can predate the Laxfordian
episode, all data known to be older than 1850 Ma are excluded. However, even this selection
is somewhat subjective because palaeomagnetic results from cross-cutting intrusions have
been variously linked to Rb-Sr isochrons or Rb-Sr and K--Ar mineral ages, and the
evidence as to whether most Lower Proterozoic anorogenic intrusions were emplaced into
country rock with regional temperatures above or below the Curie point is often of an
equivocal nature. The section of Table 3 (see Irving & McGlynn 1976; Cavenaugh & Seyfert
1977) is therefore biased towards the exclusion of pre-1850 Ma rock units which may
possess post-1 850 Ma magnetizations if this point is not adesuately clarified.

A most important study relating to Lower Proterozoic times is that of Roy & Lapointe
(1976) who identify five magnetizations (A E) from the Superior Province of which the
-+
last three are present in the Nipissing diabase dated 21 17 ? 27 and 21 10 f 80 Ma (RbSr
isochron ages); the E magnetization is remote from the earlier magnetizations and is believed
to have been acquired during the Hudsonian mobile episode (c.1 800 Ma). Poles 1, 16 and
17 (Table 3, Fig. 8) from other Provinces correspond closely with the E magnetizations; the
mutual agreement between these poles renders a tectonic explanation for poles 16 and 17
(Evans & Bingham 1976; Bingham & Evans 1976) less likely. Although the age data relating
to this group is not definitive, these data suggest that it is c.1 850-1800 and therefore
slightly older than the remaining poles in Fig. 8. These latter poles plot in a quite different
field and are in part derived from the same provinces; this large difference must leave some
doubt about the polarity of the pre-1800 Ma part of the apw curve (see Fig. 8 and Roy &
Lapointe 1976).
The 1800 to 1650Ma poles define a SE to NW trending swathe. The direction of polar
movement along this swathe is now well defined by the migration of high to low blocking
temperature components in dykes and gneisses of west Greenland (Morgan 1976a, b), the
Flin Flon primary and secondary magnetizations (poles 19 and 20, Fig. 8), the Pearson
Formation A, B and C magnetizations (30-32, Fig. 8) and possibly by the Kahocella
primary and secondary magnetizations (23 and 24, Fig. 8) for the Churchill and Bear
structural provinces. There is also good agreement between the age estimates of the poles

### page_19
Palaeomagnetism of the Lewisian foreland 119
60 Ma (Kalsbeek, Bridgwater & Zeck 1978) on the Kangamiut dykes defines a maximum
age for the magnetizations because, like the Scourie dykes, the west Greenland dyke swarms
were intruded into hot crust (Escher et al. 1976) and their magnetic blocking temperature
ranges were greatly depressed during slow uplift and cooling (Morgan 1976a, b); these
poles are now linked to K-Ar mineral and isochron ages between 1800 and 1660 Ma. The
youngest part of this swathe is defined by magnetizations from the Ketilidian mobile belt
of south Greenland linked to K-Ar and Rb-Sr mineral ages of 1700-1600 Ma (Van
Breemen, Aftalian & Allaart 1974; Piper & Stearn 1976) which also agree with two other
poles from west Greenland (9 and 12) of which the Sagdlerssuaq amphibolites have a K-Ar
isochron age of 1620k 50 Ma. This SE-NW trending part of the apw swathe is thus
confmed between the limits c. 1800-1600 Ma and the pole for the Lewisian ‘A’ magnetiza-
tions lies at the younger end of this swathe.
Several general conclusions can be drawn from the Middle Proterozoic palaeomagnetic
data of Table 3 and Fig. 8(a):
(1) Although Cavenaugh & Seyfert (1977) have utilized pre-1600 Ma data from the
Laurentian Shield to define separate apw curves for the Slave and Superior cratons, and have
proposed that the Slave and part of the Churchill province joined the remainder of the
Shield by plate collision in the Hudsonian mobile episode, their case has been strongly
criticized by Roy et al. (1978). In addition to the arguments advanced by these latter
authors, the hypothesis of Cavenaugh & Seyfert is not tenable because the poles they utilise
to define an apw path for the Slave craton are coincident with the large body of con-
temporaneous Greenlandic data (Fig. 8) from the opposite side of the Mudsonian mobile
zone.
(2) These magnetizations from the northern Churchill/Slave region are in any case not
relevant to the tectonic origin of the Hudsonian mobile episode because at least the majority
post-date the tectonic activity associated with this episode. As with the later Grenville
episode (c. 1100 Ma), the palaeomagnetic data from the mobile zone itself cannot be used to
refute an origin by plate convergence because they entirely post-date the mobile belt
tectonism. However, the agreement of poles from the Superior (14), Churchill (16, 17)
and Nain (1) provinces (Fig. 8) and certain older data (Irving & McClynn 1976; Roy et al.
1978) are strong evidence that the Laurentian Shield was already an integral unit by
1850 Ma.
(3) Although there is good overall agreement between these mid-Proterozoic palaeomagnetic
data from the constituent provinces of the Laurentian craton, there are some critical
differences and it emerges that different parts of the Shield provide complementary informa-
tion to piece together the overall apw record. Thus the earliest part of the SE -NW swathe
is well defined by a range of primary and secondary magnetizations from the Churchill and
Bear provinces; these overlap with the oldest poles from Greenland which in turn extend the
apw curve into a zone not recognized in the Churchill/Bear provinces. The youngest poles
derive from the Ketilidian and Lewisian rocks from the southern margin of the Laurentian
Shield which were being uplifted and cooled at c. 1650 Ma; comparable magnetizations to
these have not yet (with the possible exception of pole 15) been recognized in North
America.
(4) No current data from the Laurentian Shield are known with certainty to relate to the
interval 1650 1450 Ma; immediately after this the apw curve is defined by a combination
of North American (Irving & McClynn 1976; Irving, Emslie & Park 1977) and Greenlandic
(Piper 1977) results from Upper Proterozoic intrusive and supracrustal suites. The Lewisian
‘B’ magnetizations of mixed polarity correlate with these post-1450 Ma results (Fig. 8(c)).

### page_20

The Lewisian 'C' magnetizations present a greater problem: the palaeomagnetic pole both
before (258" E, 42" S) and after (229.4" E, 27.6" S) local rotation of the Lewisian complex
is accommodated does not correlate with any relevant Laurentian data (Fig. 8(c)). It does
not correlate with magnetizations from the Grenville Province (generalized in Fig. 8(c)
after McWilliams & Dunlop 1978) although a thermal/tectonic episode of this age is
recognized in the Moinian rocks to the east of the Moine Thrust zone (e.g. Brook, Brewer &
Powell 1976). It is probable that these magnetizations record later stages of the regional
uplift when the low blocking temperature phases were acquiring their remanence, and they
relate to the interval 1650-1450 Ma for which the apw curve is, as yet, undefined.
(5) As noted by Park (1975) metamorphic palaeomagnetism presents a range of problems
to which solutions may only be expected to emerge gradually. In particular, it is not yet
completely clear why some magnetizations (a) are well represented while others are poorly
defined (b) or of complex origin (c). It seems likely that such factors as initial compositions,
variable cooling rates and proximity to shear zones may be important to this problem but
they must await detailed studies for clarification.
(6) The analysis of Table 3 and Fig. 8 has been careful to exclude from consideration poles
which are older than 1850 Ma. Earlier analyses (e.g. Irving & Park 1972b) have attempted to
compress all palaeomagnetic poles assigned to the interval 2200- 1700 Ma into a single
closed apw loop. The discovery of Nipissing diabase 'E' magnetizations by Roy & Lapointe
(1976) showed that this was an oversimplified approach and resolution of this point is
critical to correlations between the Precambrian shields (Piper 1976). In the context of the
Laurentian data, it is important to distinguish those pre-1850 Ma results mostly from the
large Superior craton where it is known from the overlying pre-2300 Ma Huronian sediments
that present erosion levels had already been reached, and those post-1850 Ma results from
most of the remainder of the shield. These latter results include the Lewisian, Greenlandic
and Churchill data; although these rocks are often of Archaean origin, the present erosion
levels were at such great crustal depths during the widespread c. 1800 Ma mobile activity
that there is no possibility of an older palaeomagnetic record within them.
Acknowledgments
Precambrian palaeomagnetic studies are supported by Natural Environment Research
Council Grant GR/3/2398; I am grateful to Mrs B. Bridges and Mrs A. Wall for assistance
with the measurements and J. E. F. Stearn for help with the fieldwork. This work has
benefited greatly from discussions with Dr G. E. J. Beckmann and Dr G. E. Morgan and I
am grateful to reviewers for criticisms.
